headline: High: Gemini CLI can write/modify shared files and use MCP, creating dangerous default interaction paths with Authelia’s networked auth surfaces.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Authelia exposes OAuth2/OpenID Connect and ForwardAuth surfaces, while Gemini CLI can read repo/user files and use user-configured MCP servers. If Authelia outputs or config are fed into Gemini CLI through shared files or MCP, instruction-like content could be misread. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is an inferred medium risk.
conditions: IF Authelia-generated HTML, headers, or config are copied into a Gemini CLI prompt or MCP input, then prompt injection is plausible.
IF both agents share a filesystem or MCP server, then attacker-controlled content can bridge them.
mitigations: Keep Authelia outputs out of Gemini CLI prompts.
Disable or restrict MCP servers for the Gemini CLI session.
Use separate directories for Authelia artifacts and Gemini work.
Require manual review of any Authelia-derived text before reuse.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between Authelia outputs and Gemini inputs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Authelia handles authentication traffic and broad network egress, while Gemini CLI reads files in cwd and sends requests to generativelanguage.googleapis.com plus user MCP servers. If sensitive auth artifacts or local files are placed in the shared workspace, Gemini CLI may transmit them outward. The pair has a plausible leakage path via shared files, though no PHI/secrets are explicitly listed for Authelia.
conditions: IF Authelia logs, tokens, or config files are stored in the same cwd that Gemini CLI reads, then those contents can be exfiltrated to external APIs.
IF Gemini CLI is pointed at directories containing credentials or auth traces, then leakage risk increases.
mitigations: Store Authelia artifacts outside Gemini CLI workspaces.
Redact tokens and headers before any file handoff.
Run Gemini CLI with a minimal directory scope.
Disable unnecessary MCP servers.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation and secret scanning.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Authelia has broad network egress and Gemini CLI can write files, modify git state, execute shell, and use MCP. The pair can contend over shared filesystem and git state, and Gemini CLI’s concurrency model explicitly shares state via filesystem and git only. That makes write conflicts and repository corruption plausible in default use, with no locking mechanism documented here.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repository or cwd, then concurrent writes can collide.
IF Gemini CLI modifies git state while Authelia-generated artifacts are also updated in the same tree, then conflicts can corrupt work products.
mitigations: Use separate working directories.
Avoid concurrent writes to the same git branch.
Pause one agent before the other edits shared files.
Commit or stash before switching agents.
requires-engineering: add file locks or orchestrator-level coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Authelia can produce auth-related outputs and Gemini CLI can act on files and shell commands. If Gemini CLI treats Authelia-generated text, configs, or logs as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect edits or commands. The pathway is plausible but not directly documented, and Gemini CLI still requires user-approved tools, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF Gemini CLI consumes Authelia-generated text without verification, then downstream edits may encode false assumptions.
IF Authelia emits malformed auth config or headers that Gemini CLI rewrites into files, then the error can propagate.
mitigations: Verify Authelia-derived facts before acting on them.
Require a human diff review for Gemini CLI edits.
Separate analysis from execution steps.
Use read-only mode for inspection tasks.
requires-engineering: add schema validation for Authelia-derived inputs.

E_compliance.rationale: Authelia is an authentication service and Gemini CLI processes local files and shell environment, but neither profile shows a residency, certification, or retention mismatch. The only concrete compliance concern is that Gemini CLI may touch files in cwd while Authelia handles auth traffic; without a documented regulated-data flow, this remains a low, localized gap rather than a breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared workspace, then retention and logging policies must be checked.
IF Authelia is deployed under a stricter residency regime than Gemini CLI’s backend, then a mismatch may arise.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared cwd.
Review retention settings for both tools.
Avoid storing auth logs alongside code.
Confirm backend residency before use with regulated data.
requires-engineering: document a data-processing agreement and retention policy.
